title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) in Graph Traversal
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement Breadth-First Search (BFS) to discover the shortest path in an unweighted graph from a given starting vertex to a target destination.
theory: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores all vertices of a graph layer by layer, visiting immediate neighbors before moving to vertices at the next depth level. BFS guarantees finding the shortest path (in terms of edge count) in unweighted graphs. It uses a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue.
algorithm: Initialize an empty FIFO queue and enqueue the start vertex.
Maintain a visited set to avoid infinite loops and cycles.
Track parent pointers in a dictionary to reconstruct the traversed path.
While the queue is not empty, dequeue the current node.
If current node matches the goal, backtrack along parent pointers to reconstruct the path.
Otherwise, for each unvisited neighbor of current node, mark as visited, record its parent, and enqueue it.
If the queue empties without reaching the goal, report that no path exists.
timeComplexity: O(V + E) where V is vertices and E is edges
spaceComplexity: O(V) to store queue and visited set
inputDescription: Start node letter (e.g. A) on first line, Target goal letter (e.g. J) on second line.
sampleOutput:

Enter starting letter: a
Enter target goal letter: j

Path found from A to J:
A -> C -> F -> J

title: Greedy Best-First Search with Heuristics
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement Greedy Best-First Search using a heuristic evaluation function h(n) = |ord(goal) - ord(node)| to navigate from a start node to a goal node.
theory: Greedy Best-First Search is an informed search strategy that expands the node deemed closest to the goal based solely on an evaluation heuristic h(n). Unlike BFS, it uses a Priority Queue ordered by h(n). While fast and memory-efficient in practice, it is not guaranteed to find the globally optimal path because it ignores accumulated path cost g(n).
algorithm: Define a heuristic function h(n) estimating the distance from node n to the goal.
Initialize a Priority Queue with the start node prioritized by h(start, goal).
Maintain a visited set to avoid redundant expansion.
While the priority queue is not empty, extract the node with the lowest heuristic value.
If the extracted node is the goal node, return the accumulated path.
If not yet visited, mark as visited and evaluate all its unvisited neighbors with h(neighbor, goal).
Insert each valid neighbor with its updated path into the priority queue.
timeComplexity: O(b^m) worst-case where b is branching factor and m is maximum depth
spaceComplexity: O(b^m) to hold the priority queue and visited states
inputDescription: Start letter (A-J) on first line, Target goal letter (A-J) on second line.
sampleOutput:

Enter target goal letter (A-J): j

Path found from A to J:

title: Depth-First Search (DFS) in Graph Traversal
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement Depth-First Search (DFS) using a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack to explore paths deeply before backtracking.
theory: Depth-First Search (DFS) systematically explores as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking. It requires less memory than BFS when solutions are deep and plentiful, using O(b * m) space. However, it is neither complete on infinite graphs nor guaranteed to find the shortest path.
algorithm: Initialize a LIFO stack containing the start node and its initial path.
Maintain a visited set to prevent cyclic loops.
While the stack is not empty, pop the top node and its path.
If the popped node is the target goal, return the path.
If the node has not been visited, add it to the visited set.
Push all unvisited neighbors along with their appended path onto the stack.
spaceComplexity: O(V) proportional to maximum search depth

title: Greedy Heuristic Search on Custom State Graphs
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Demonstrate heuristic guided search using an explicit predefined heuristic table h(n) on tree-like hierarchical state graphs.
theory: In heuristic graph search, domain-specific estimates h(n) guide the frontier expansion towards the goal. The algorithm prioritizes nodes with the smallest estimated distance to the target state.
algorithm: Create a priority queue containing (h(start), start, [start]).
Extract the state with minimum heuristic value.
If state is goal, terminate and return path.
Otherwise expand children, compute their respective heuristics, and enqueue them.
timeComplexity: O(b^d) where d is depth of goal
inputDescription: Starting node letter on first line, Goal node letter on second line.
code:
graph = {
    'A': ['B', 'C'],
    'B': ['D', 'E'],
    'C': ['F', 'G'],
    'D': ['H', 'I'],
    'E': ['J'],
    'F': [],
    'G': [],
    'H': [],
    'I': [],
    'J': []
}

heuristic = {
    'A': 3,
    'B': 2,
    'C': 10,
    'D': 5,
    'E': 1,
    'F': 11,
    'G': 12,
    'H': 6,
    'I': 7,
    'J': 0
}

def heuristic_search(start, goal):
    current = start
    path = [current]

    while current != goal:
        neighbors = graph[current]

        if not neighbors:
            print("Goal not found!")
            return


        current = min(neighbors, key=lambda x: heuristic[x])
        path.append(current)

    print("\nGoal Found!")
    print("Path:")
    print(" -> ".join(path))

start = input("Enter the starting node: ").upper()
goal = input("Enter the goal node: ").upper()

if start in graph and goal in graph:
    heuristic_search(start, goal)
else:
    print("Invalid node!")

title: A* Search Algorithm (Optimal Cost + Admissible Heuristic)
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement the A* algorithm combining exact path cost g(n) and heuristic estimate h(n) using f(n) = g(n) + h(n) to guarantee optimal pathfinding.
theory: A* is one of the most widely used algorithms for pathfinding and graph traversal. It evaluates nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the exact cost from the start node to n, and h(n) is the estimated cost from n to the goal. When h(n) is admissible (never overestimates the true cost) and consistent, A* is both complete and strictly optimal.
algorithm: Initialize an open list (min-heap) with (f(start), g(start), start, path).
Maintain a dictionary of lowest g-costs discovered for each node.
While open list is not empty, pop the element with lowest f(n).
If current node is goal, return the optimal path and total path cost g.
For each neighbor with edge weight w, compute tentative_g = g + w.
If tentative_g is lower than any previously recorded g for this neighbor:
Update lowest_g, calculate f = tentative_g + h(neighbor), and push to open list.
timeComplexity: O(E) in best case, O(b^d) in worst case
spaceComplexity: O(b^d) to store all generated nodes in open/closed lists
inputDescription: Start Node (e.g. A) on first line, Goal Node (e.g. J) on second line.
code:
import heapq

graph = {
    'A': [('B', 1), ('C', 3)],
    'B': [('D', 3), ('E', 2)],
    'C': [('F', 4)],
    'D': [],
    'E': [('G', 1)],
    'F': [],
    'G': [('H', 1)],
    'H': [('I', 1)],
    'I': [('J', 1)],
    'J': []
}

heuristic = {
    'A': 7,
    'B': 6,
    'C': 7,
    'D': 3,
    'E': 4,
    'F': 3,
    'G': 3,
    'H': 2,
    'I': 1,
    'J': 0
}

def astar(start, goal):

    if start not in graph or start not in heuristic:
        print(f"Error: Start node '{start}' is not in the graph")
        return
    if goal not in graph or goal not in heuristic:
        print(f"Error: Goal node '{goal}' is not in the graph")
        return

    pq = [(heuristic[start], 0, start, [start])]
    visited = set()

    while pq:
        f, cost, node, path = heapq.heappop(pq)

        if node == goal:
            print("Shortest Path:")
            print(" -> ".join(path))
            print("Cost =", cost)
            return

        if node not in visited:
            visited.add(node)

            for neighbor, c in graph[node]:
                if neighbor not in visited:
                    heapq.heappush(
                        pq,
                        (cost + c + heuristic[neighbor],
                         cost + c,
                         neighbor,
                         path + [neighbor])
                    )

    print(f"No path found from {start} to {goal}.")

start_node_input = input("Enter Start Node: ").upper()
goal_node_input = input("Enter Goal Node: ").upper()

astar(start_node_input, goal_node_input)

title: AO* Search Algorithm (AND/OR Graph Heuristics)
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement the AO* algorithm to find optimal solution subtrees in problem-reduction AND/OR graphs.
theory: AO* is a heuristic search algorithm designed for AND/OR graphs, which model problems decomposable into independent subproblems. An OR node succeeds if ANY of its branches succeeds. An AND node requires ALL of its branches to succeed. AO* recursively updates node heuristics and marks solved states until an optimal solution graph is verified.
algorithm: Create tree nodes initialized with heuristic estimates and solved=False.
Traverse from the root down the current best partial tree.
Identify unexpanded non-terminal leaf nodes.
Expand leaf nodes, evaluate their AND/OR successors, and propagate revised costs backward.
Mark branches as solved when all sub-goals under an AND branch or any branch under an OR node are solved.
Continue iterations until the root node is marked solved.
timeComplexity: O(b^d) where b is AND/OR branching factor
spaceComplexity: O(V) to maintain explicit search tree
inputDescription: Self-contained graph definition. No standard input required.
code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, name, heuristic=0):
        self.name = name
        self.heuristic = heuristic
        self.solved = False
        self.children = []


def ao_star(node):


    if node.name == "J":
        node.solved = True
        node.heuristic = 0
        return

    if not node.children:
        return

    best_cost = float('inf')
    best_group = None


    for group in node.children:
        cost = sum(edge_cost + child.heuristic
                   for child, edge_cost in group)

        if cost < best_cost:
            best_cost = cost
            best_group = group


    for child, edge_cost in best_group:
        ao_star(child)

    node.heuristic = sum(
        edge_cost + child.heuristic
        for child, edge_cost in best_group
    )


    if all(child.solved for child, edge_cost in best_group):
        node.solved = True


def print_solution(node, level=0):

    print("  " * level + node.name)

    if node.name == "J" or not node.children:
        return

    best_cost = float('inf')
    best_group = None

    for group in node.children:

        cost = sum(
            edge_cost + child.heuristic
            for child, edge_cost in group
        )

        if cost < best_cost:
            best_cost = cost
            best_group = group

    for child, edge_cost in best_group:
        print_solution(child, level + 1)

title: Alpha-Beta Pruning in Adversarial Game Trees
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement Alpha-Beta Pruning to optimize the Minimax decision rule in 2-player zero-sum game trees by eliminating subtrees that cannot influence the final decision.
theory: Alpha-Beta pruning maintains two bounds during recursive depth-first minimax evaluation: Alpha (the highest value that the MAX player has secured along the path) and Beta (the lowest value that the MIN player has secured). Whenever Alpha >= Beta, the opponent would never allow this branch to be chosen, so the remaining child subtrees are pruned immediately.
algorithm: Initialize Alpha = -inf and Beta = +inf at the root of the game tree.
At terminal depth, return the static evaluation value of the leaf node.
For a MAX node: iterate through children, recursively call alphabeta with minimizing flag.
Update best = max(best, value), and Alpha = max(Alpha, best).
If Beta <= Alpha, cut off remaining siblings (Beta cutoff).
For a MIN node: iterate through children, recursively call alphabeta with maximizing flag.
Update best = min(best, value), and Beta = min(Beta, best).
If Beta <= Alpha, cut off remaining siblings (Alpha cutoff).
timeComplexity: O(b^(d/2)) with optimal move ordering, down from O(b^d) in plain Minimax
spaceComplexity: O(d) depth of the game tree
inputDescription: Self-contained binary game tree with leaf valuations. No input required.
code:
def alphabeta(depth, node, maximizing, values, alpha, beta):
    if depth == 3:
        return values[node]

    if maximizing:
        best = -999
        for i in range(2):
            value = alphabeta(depth + 1, node * 2 + i,
                              False, values, alpha, beta)
            best = max(best, value)
            alpha = max(alpha, best)

            if beta <= alpha:
                break

        return best

    else:
        best = 999
        for i in range(2):
            value = alphabeta(depth + 1, node * 2 + i,
                              True, values, alpha, beta)
            best = min(best, value)
            beta = min(beta, best)

            if beta <= alpha:
                break

        return best



values = [3, 5, 6, 9, 1, 2, 0, -1]

alpha = -999
beta = 999

result = alphabeta(0, 0, True, values, alpha, beta)

print("Optimal Value:", result)

title: N-Queens Problem (Backtracking & Constraint Satisfaction)
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Place N non-attacking queens on an N×N chessboard such that no two queens share the same row, column, or diagonal.
theory: The N-Queens puzzle is a classic Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP). Backtracking incrementally builds candidates to the solutions, abandoning a candidate ("backtracking") as soon as it determines that the candidate cannot possibly be completed to a valid placement.
algorithm: Start in the leftmost column / top row.
If all queens are placed (row == N), a valid solution configuration is reached.
Try all columns in the current row: for each column col:
Check if the position (row, col) is safe from existing queens on same column or diagonals (|board[i] - col| == |i - row|).
If safe, place queen and recursively attempt to solve row + 1.
If placing queen leads to no solution, remove queen (backtrack) and try the next column.
spaceComplexity: O(N) to store queen row positions and recursion stack

title: 8-Puzzle Solver with A* (Misplaced Tiles vs Manhattan Distance)
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Solve the 8-Puzzle sliding tile problem using A* search and evaluate the performance of Misplaced Tiles (h1) versus Manhattan Distance (h2).
theory: The 8-Puzzle consists of a 3x3 board with 8 numbered tiles and an empty space. Comparing heuristics: h1 counts the number of misplaced tiles, while h2 computes the sum of Manhattan distances of tiles from their goal positions. Because h2 dominates h1 (h2(n) >= h1(n) for all n), A* with Manhattan distance explores strictly fewer or equal nodes while still maintaining admissibility.
algorithm: Represent state as 9-tuple representing 3x3 board with 0 as blank space.
Compute h1 (count mismatches with goal) and h2 (sum |row - goal_row| + |col - goal_col|).
Run A* using h1 and record nodes generated and total moves.
Run A* using h2 and record nodes generated and total moves.
Print formatted comparison table showing search efficiency differences.
spaceComplexity: O(b^d) priority queue and visited states set

title: Interactive Tic-Tac-Toe AI with Minimax and Alpha-Beta Table
subject: Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
objective: Implement an unbeatable Tic-Tac-Toe AI engine utilizing Minimax with Alpha-Beta pruning, logging every decision node, alpha/beta window, and cutoff.
theory: Tic-Tac-Toe has a game-tree complexity that allows full depth evaluation. Applying Alpha-Beta pruning reduces the number of evaluated terminal nodes significantly while guaranteeing the computer never loses (achieving optimal play: win or draw).
algorithm: Represent 3x3 board as a 9-element list (indices 0 through 8).
On AI turn, invoke find_best_move() which tests all legal empty squares.
Run minimax(depth, is_maximizing, alpha, beta) recursively.
Log search table with depth, stage (MAX/MIN), move, value, alpha, beta, and Cutoff status.
Execute moves interactively with the user until victory or draw.
